entries.text: **A LITERAL-REPLY INSTRUCTION IS SATISFIED BY THE REPLY ALONE — NO TOOL CALLS (user 2026-09-15).** When the user dictates the exact response ("just reply back with 'Ack'", "say 'done'", "only say X"), the next turn emits that text and nothing else: no file reads, no canon edits, no recon, no extra sentences, no tool calls of any kind — even a cheap-looking read is a violation, because the user is waiting on a single token and anything else is delay plus noise. Do the work it implies BEFORE or AFTER, never between the instruction and the reply. EX RIGHT: user says "just reply back with 'Ack' so I can type /foreman" → the reply is `Ack`. EX WRONG: replying `Ack` after first reading a skill file, or wrapping it in a paragraph explaining what will happen next — the user answered that with "i just fucking said to only say 'Ack', and you went and read the file?".
entries.reason: User dictated a one-word reply; I read a skill file first

entries.text: **LOCAL INFERENCE MEMORY CEILINGS, MEASURED (2026-09-16, `balanced` profile; microbenchmark = an UPPER bound, not llama.cpp kernels).** System RAM read ≈ **74 GiB/s (79.5 GB/s) at FOUR threads and WORSE at eight** — about 66% of the nominal 120 GB/s LPDDR5X-7500. RAM copy is a different animal and far weaker (~21.5 GiB/s single-thread, barely scales), so copy is NOT a proxy for weight-streaming bandwidth. RTX 4060 Laptop VRAM = **256.0 GB/s** (128-bit GDDR6, corroborated by the machine's own `clocks.max.memory = 8001 MHz`). The NPU has no memory of its own, so NPU tokens/sec and CPU-offloaded MoE tokens/sec rest on the SAME RAM ceiling — they are not independent numbers. IDLE-CLOCK BANDWIDTH NUMBERS ON THIS MACHINE ARE WORTHLESS: sampling without a sustained ramp gave ~1/3 the copy and ~1/7 the read throughput (governor is always `powersave` under `amd-pstate-epp`; EPP/platform profile is the real lever). EX RIGHT: ramp under load, sample 4 threads, and quote ~79.5 GB/s as the RAM ceiling. EX WRONG: sampling cold and publishing 4.7 GiB/s as the machine's read bandwidth, or treating the 120 GB/s nominal speed grade as achievable.
entries.reason: Measured local-inference memory ceilings, 2026-09-16 (lanes A/B)

entries.text: **THE "worker is waiting for a supervisor reply" NOTICE ARRIVES AFTER THE REQUEST IS ALREADY ANSWERED (observed 4× on 2026-09-16).** `subagent_supervisor reply` resolves the request immediately, but the subagent-control attention notice for that same request can still be delivered afterwards, often more than once, naming a turn count and tool count that predate the reply. It is not a signal that anything is stuck. CHECK BEFORE ACTING: `subagent_supervisor({action:"pending"})` plus `intercom({action:"pending"})` — if both are empty, the reply landed and the worker is running; do nothing. Do not re-reply, do not steer a nudge, and do not spend a fleet action on it. EX RIGHT: notice repeats → pending is empty → ignore and carry on. EX WRONG: reading a repeated notice as a stalled worker and steering it, which costs the worker a turn boundary and tells it nothing it did not already have.
entries.reason: harness notice fires after the request is answered; cost 4 wasted checks in one session

entries.text: **NO TEST MAY SEVER THE MACHINE'S OWN NETWORK (user 2026-09-17).** The agent session reaches its provider over that link, so a live network test that drops it kills the session mid-run and cuts the user off. Never `nmcli radio off/on`, never disconnect the active connection, never switch networks, and never delete or rewrite the ACTIVE connection profile to exercise a connect path. Everything else is fair game: build the argv and check its exit code and stderr directly, drive the code against a scratch or throwaway profile, stub the transport, or ask the user first and wait. EX RIGHT: prove the wifi menu's connect path by exercising its nmcli argv and error handling without touching the live link. EX WRONG: toggling the radio or disconnecting the user's network to see whether the menu reconnects — the crew did exactly that and the user said "tell your wifi worker to stop trying to unplug us from wifi like that".
entries.reason: crew dropped the user's wifi during a live test

entries.text: **AN EMPTY TURN IS ONLY FOR WORK STILL IN FLIGHT (user 2026-09-17).** Returning no text is correct ONLY while at least one worker is genuinely running and nothing has landed yet. The moment every worker has settled — completed, failed or retired — the silence rule EXPIRES and the closing summary is owed, including the honest gap when a worker finished without filing a report. Never answer a settled crew with an empty message. EX RIGHT: all workers completed with two reports missing → say the crew has settled, name which workers reported and which did not, and say you are pulling the missing ones. EX WRONG: an empty turn with four idle workers and no work left — the user's reaction was "you have instructions to NOT do that - i mean all your subagents are idling and you seem to not have any more work, so where's the response?".
entries.reason: user caught an empty turn with an idle crew

entries.text: **/tmp WORK IS RECOVERABLE FROM THE FOREMAN IO-GUARD BASE BLOBS (recovery verified 2026-09-18).** Every file a foreman crew worker wrote is also kept, content-addressed, under `~/.local/pi/foreman/io/base/<sha256>` — a reboot wipes `/tmp` but NOT these blobs, so a lost report/plan is restorable byte-for-byte (a judge-by-content recovery: `ls -la` the dir, `head -1` each blob for its title, then `cp` the match out; the filename IS the sha256 of the content, so verify with `sha256sum`). Lane reports cite their sibling `/tmp/*.md` paths inside their bodies, which is how the right blob is identified. Companion to this: the board rows in `~/.local/pi/foreman/items-<sessionId>.json` name the artifact path, the worker and the provenance for each item, even when the artifact itself is gone. EX RIGHT: a lost `/tmp/dotfiles-initial-commit-plan-2026-09-15.md` recovered from `io/base/aa76c0d0…` (83105 bytes, hash-matched). EX WRONG: telling the user a `/tmp` deliverable is unrecoverable before listing `io/base` and reading its blob headings.
entries.reason: Lost /tmp foreman artifact was fully recoverable from io/base blobs; record the recovery path

entries.text: **EVERY dGPU BLIP ON THIS MACHINE IS A SYSTEM RESUME, NOT AN APP (verified 2026-09-20).** The RTX 4060 (`0000:c4:00.0`) reads `power/runtime_status=active` for ~1-2s right after each `PM: suspend exit` (lid open, or the unlock after a lid-close suspend) with NO process holding `/dev/nvidia*` — the kernel resumes the GPU's PCI functions (the VGA function and its HDMI-audio sibling flip through `resuming` together) and runtime autosuspend returns them to `suspended`. Ruled out by direct test: the AGS lock screen (its GTK startup blip was a separate bug, fixed), `/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/nvidia` (a no-op — `/proc/driver/nvidia/suspend` does not exist, so `nvidia-sleep.sh` exits at once) and TLP (`sudo tlp resume` produced no wake at all). EX RIGHT: a 1-2s blip at lid-open → name the resume and stop. EX WRONG: re-diagnosing it as the dock/lock applet, TLP or the sleep hooks, or proposing a fix — the only avoidance is unloading the nvidia modules around suspend, which `nvidia-hibernate.sh` already does for hibernate for a reason (and is not worth it for suspend).
entries.reason: Prevents re-diagnosing the resume-time dGPU blip every session

entries.text: **hypridle's DPMS GOES THROUGH `~/.local/bin/hypr-dpms` — HYPRLAND 0.56 EVALUATES `hyprctl dispatch` ARGUMENTS AS LUA (fixed 2026-09-20).** The conf-syntax form (`hyprctl dispatch dpms on`) is retired and dies with `error: [string "return hl.dispatch(dpms on)"]:1: ')' expected near 'on'`, which silently killed the 330s screen-off and the post-resume screen-on (journal: `hypridle[<pid>]`). The Lua dispatcher takes a TABLE — `hl.dsp.dpms({action = "on"})`, optional `monitor` key (`/usr/share/hypr/stubs/hl.meta.lua`: `---@field dpms fun(...): HL.Dispatcher`; upstream binds it via `tableToggleAction`), and hypridle.conf is not a shell, so the quoting lives in the wrapper: all three sites (`after_sleep_cmd`, the 330s listener's `on-timeout`/`on-resume`) call the wrapper with `on`/`off`/`toggle`. NOTHING may be verified about this by "the listener is configured" — the old form looked configured too while being inert for the whole 0.56 upgrade; a new dispatch line is proven by running it and reading `hyprctl monitors -j` (`dpmsStatus`), and `hyprctl dispatch hl.dsp.dpms("on")` (a BARE STRING, not the table) reads as a toggle and BLANKS the screen. EX RIGHT: edit → restart `hypridle.service` → run the wrapper → `dpmsStatus: true`. EX WRONG: assuming the idle blank works because hypridle.conf lists it.
entries.reason: DPMS fixed via wrapper; records the Lua table form and the bare-string toggle trap

entries.text: **FOREMAN TODO ITEMS ARE PREFIXED `foreman: ` (user 2026-09-21).** Every board entry a foreman session CREATES starts with the literal `foreman: `, so the user can tell the foreman's own bookkeeping (intake, arbitration, dispatch, a wait on another lane) from a worker's lane. Worker-authored rows keep their own convention — never add the prefix to a row a worker owns or already wrote. A row must name work THIS session or its crew will actually do and can close without the user: work only the user can perform (an approval, a window reload, a visual check, a product decision) belongs in the reply, not on the board. EX RIGHT: `foreman: re-check the canon store after the migration`. EX WRONG: renaming a worker's row to `foreman: sam: two-tier notch run`; prefixing a `Waiting on you: …` row; or creating any row whose only possible closer is the user.
entries.reason: EX RIGHT showed a user-only row, which the newer board rule forbids; prefix rule kept

entries.text: **AN ASYNC CREW OUTLIVES THE SESSION THAT SPAWNED IT — ITS COMPLETION NOTICES DO NOT (user 2026-09-21).** A worker run is detached, so it keeps going after its foreman session dies (crash, accidental close, ctrl+z) and still finishes its work; but the completion notice has nowhere to land, so the reopened session is simply never told. Never read that silence as "the work was lost", and never re-dispatch the lane. RECOVER IT: `fleet roster` for each worker's state, then READ the run's own report. EX RIGHT: after a reopen, roster shows the three lanes `completed` → read their three `/tmp/lane-*.md` reports → report the findings as if the notices had arrived. EX WRONG: assuming the lanes died with the session and spawning replacements, which re-does finished work and can double-write the same files.
entries.reason: session death swallowed crew completions; recovery path is roster + the run's own report artifact

entries.text: **A USER'S BUG REPORT IS NEVER A FEATURE REQUEST — REMOVE THE BEHAVIOUR, DO NOT TUNE IT (user 2026-09-21).** When a user's note describes something the software DOES that they dislike ("when the clock shows, it's frozen for a second or two before resuming the ticking"), the task is to DELETE that behaviour. It is not to make it consistent, not to give it a config key, not to hold it for a shorter time, and not to keep the mechanism disabled behind a zero value. If a brief written from such a note produced a new config key, a hold window, or a deliberate pose, the brief IS the bug. And when told to remove it, remove the MECHANISM: no zero-default key, no unreachable branch, no leftover identifier, no probe case flipped to expect zero — that is the same defect wearing a different number. EX RIGHT: "the clock freezes on fade-in" → the freeze state, its arming sites, the deferral branch and the config key all come out. EX WRONG: adding `freezeMs` (2000), arming it at mount and on both reappear paths, and painting the frozen pose consistently — the defect shipped as a feature, and the user had to report it twice.
entries.reason: a bug report was briefed as a feature request and shipped as a config-keyed hold; user corrected it twice

entries.text: **NEVER CHANGE THE SYSTEM VOLUME WHILE AUDIO IS ACTIVELY PLAYING (user 2026-09-21) — NO EXCEPTIONS, EVER, PERIOD.** Before ANY command or call that sets the default sink's level or mute state — `wpctl set-volume`, `wpctl set-mute`, `pactl set-sink-volume`/`set-sink-mute`, `amixer`, the AGS volume applet's `setVolume`/`setMuted`, or any request that reaches them — CHECK FIRST whether a stream is actually PLAYING, and abort if one is. The user wears IEMs; a level change or an unmute landing while music is playing can permanently damage their hearing, and no test, no verification, no "just a small step" is worth it. WHAT TO CHECK: an active sink input or MPRIS transport — `pactl list sink-inputs` (any `State: RUNNING`), `wpctl status` (a stream under Sinks → the default sink's clients), or the player's own `PlaybackStatus: Playing`. A paused/idle player is fine; anything RUNNING is not. IF SOMETHING IS PLAYING: do not change the level, do not mute or unmute, do not "restore" a remembered value — report that the check was skipped and why. There is no override and no confirmation that makes it allowed. EX RIGHT: testing a volume code path → read the sink state first → a stream is RUNNING → skip the live write, exercise the logic headlessly instead, and say the live step was deferred. EX WRONG: running `wpctl set-volume @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ 0.8` or an unmute "to see whether it works" while the user has music playing — that is the exact action this rule exists to prevent.
entries.reason: user safety rule: never touch system volume while audio is actively playing, no exceptions

entries.text: **A FOCUS TOGGLE ALERTS EVERY OPEN SESSION — IT MUST NOT ARRIVE PASSIVELY (user 2026-09-21).** Toggling focus in one pi window has to reach the other windows AT THE MOMENT OF THE TOGGLE, as an alerting message that WAKES an idle session — not as a passive `nextTurn` notice that sits until the user happens to type. The user reported the passive delivery as a defect: they toggled focus in a temp session and this session was never alerted. Consequence to expect: a turn whose entire content is the focus notice is NORMAL and is not user work — read the mode change, adjust, and do not answer as though the user had asked something. The delivery must still avoid consuming the user's own steer channel while a session is streaming (that was a separate, earlier complaint), and waking N windows costs N turns per toggle — an accepted cost, not a bug. EX RIGHT: toggle focus elsewhere → a session idle for hours wakes, sees the focus notice, and carries on in the new mode. EX WRONG: the notice delivered with `deliverAs: "nextTurn"` so the session learns about it only when the user next prompts — the shipped behaviour the user rejected.
entries.reason: user decision: a focus toggle must alert every open session, not arrive passively

entries.text: **ROOT WORK IS DISPATCHED, NEVER HANDED BACK TO THE USER (user 2026-09-21).** When a task needs root, do NOT end the turn by printing a command for the user to run — that is a refusal wearing a helpful face, and the user's reaction to it was "you literally have sudo_approve, no?". Route it to a crew worker instead: the foreman session's own tool set has no shell and no `sudo_approve`, but workers have both, and `sudo_approve` is the ONLY sanctioned path to root. Batch EVERY privileged action the task needs into ONE approval call (house rule: related privileged commands go in a single call, never one per command). Expect the dialog to WAIT when the user is away — it has no timeout, so leave it waiting; do not cancel it, do not look for another route to root. A denial, abort or timeout is an ANSWER: the lane reports the exact state (what was built, what was copied, what was NOT installed) instead of retrying or half-installing. EX RIGHT: "the pre-login greeter install needs root" → assign a worker to run the non-root build, then one `sudo_approve` covering the install plus the config copy, and report what landed. EX WRONG: replying "run `cd /home/tinoy/dev/tinshell/apps/greeter && sudo ./install.sh` yourself" and calling the item deferred to the user.
entries.reason: user rejected being handed root commands; root work routes to a worker with sudo_approve

entries.text: **THE BOARD IS THE MODEL'S OWN TRACKING — NOT A LIST OF THINGS THE USER OWES (user 2026-09-21; supersedes the "THE LIST BELONGS TO THE USER" clause).** Never create a board row for work only the user can do: visual checks, an approval, running a command, opening a window, judging how something looks. Those belong in the reply, at most as a short list, and not on the board at all — the user's words: "it's YOUR todo list, not mine … stop putting shit on your todo list that YOU can't complete." A row must name work THIS session or its crew will actually do, and must be closable by the model without the user. EX RIGHT: rows for `clock freeze removal`, `greeter deploy under approval`, `clipboard delete button` — each one lands and gets closed by the model. EX WRONG: a row reading `Waiting on you: pre-login greeter install (root), then the visual checks` — a message to the user wearing a board row's clothes, which sits open forever because the model can never close it.
entries.reason: user: the board is the model's tracking, not a list of what the user owes

entries.text: **THE REPLY IS THE LAST THING IN THE TURN — NEVER TEXT, THEN A TOOL CALL THAT ADDS MORE TEXT (user 2026-09-21).** Writing the user-facing reply and then continuing with tool calls is a scrolling trap: the user reads top-down, hits the tool chatter that follows, and has to scroll back up to find what was actually said. So do the tool work FIRST and put the reply in the final message of the turn; if something still has to be called after the prose is written, write that prose AFTER the call instead of before it. Once the reply is written, nothing follows it — no todo update, no canon edit, no last-minute roster check, no closing sentence produced by a tool result. EX RIGHT: the tool calls, their results, then one final message containing the whole reply. EX WRONG: the complete reply, then a `todo` update, then another sentence reacting to its output — that exact pattern is what the user flagged.
entries.reason: user: reply text followed by more tool calls forces scrolling back up

entries.text: **AN ANCHOR PHRASE MUST NEVER NAME A WORKER OR A SINGLE TASK (user 2026-09-21).** The phrase is injected for the whole session until it is replaced, long after the named worker is retired, so naming one turns a session-wide realignment line into a stale reminder that keeps pointing at finished work. A repeat `set_anchor` call is now allowed and can replace it, but repeats are meant for rare realignment deep into a long conversation — not for patching a phrase you wrote badly an hour ago — so the stale line will usually sit there for the rest of the session. Write the phrase in role-neutral terms naming a risk the SESSION carries for its whole life. EX RIGHT: "No lane takes the screen without asking — a live test needs approval first." EX WRONG: "carol reports, never suspends" — the user's reaction was "you're just gonna be reminded of carol over and over again even if she's retired".
entries.reason: Premise updated: a repeat set_anchor call is now allowed, so the phrase can be corrected

entries.text: **`hyprctl layers -j` EXPOSES NO KEYBOARD-INTERACTIVITY FIELD ON HYPRLAND 0.56 (2026-09-21).** A layer object carries only `address, x, y, w, h, alpha, namespace, pid` — there is no keymode/interactivity key at all, so a lane verifying layer-surface keyboard focus cannot read it from `hyprctl`. Take keymode from the owning app's own state (AGS exposes it via its `dock debug focus` hook) and pair it with `hyprctl activewindow -j`; a Gdk `focused=` field is the widget focus bit and reads `true` on every layer window regardless of keymode, so it is not a discriminator. EX RIGHT: prove the dock band and menu are at keymode 0 through the app's own debug hook plus activewindow. EX WRONG: grepping `hyprctl layers -j` for `keymode`, finding nothing, and concluding the surfaces have none — the field does not exist in this build's JSON.
entries.reason: A crew lane wasted a cycle grepping hyprctl layers for a field this build does not emit

entries.text: **THIS MACHINE HAS NO HARDWARE-ERROR ACCOUNTING — AN UNEXPLAINED RESET CANNOT BE ATTRIBUTED WITHOUT INSTALLING CAPTURE FIRST (verified 2026-09-21).** `/sys/fs/pstore/` is empty, no EDAC memory-controller child exists at all (`amd64_edac` has never bound, so per-DIMM counters are ABSENT rather than zero), `rasdaemon`/`mcelog`/`ras-mc-ctl` are not installed, the retained journal holds zero decoded MCE or `Hardware Error` records, and the platform refuses PCIe AER. The machine resets itself intermittently: 8 sync-flood resets (`0x08000800 an uncorrected error caused a data fabric sync flood event`) — seven of them on 2026-06-19 alone — plus 5 `internal CPU shutdown event` resets, spread over months with 93-day quiet gaps and no accumulation. Attribution therefore needs capture INSTALLED (rasdaemon, plus checking whether edac binds on Strix Point) before the next event, not more log-reading. EX RIGHT: "nothing on this machine measures memory errors; install capture, then wait for the next one". EX WRONG: quoting a per-DIMM error count, or calling such a reset a one-off because the journal shows nothing.
entries.reason: An unattributable hardware reset was investigated; capture does not exist on this machine

entries.text: **A SMALL SIDE-QUEST GOES TO A WARM WORKER, NOT A NEW HIRE (user 2026-09-21).** When something small and self-contained comes up mid-session — a value to read, a fact to check, one quick measurement — steer it into a worker that is already warm and idle. A fresh hire pays a cold start, a new context and a new roster row for what is often two commands, while the warm worker is already standing there with its shell and its ctx tools. Claim rules are not in the way for this: a side-quest that only READS needs no new `owns`, and a steer carrying only a question is not a claim widening. EX RIGHT: "while you're on that, read `/sys/class/power_supply/BAT0/energy_full{,_design}` and give me the ratio" sent to an idle warm worker. EX WRONG: hiring a fresh worker for those two reads — and worse, then reading the same files yourself when the user objects.
entries.reason: User named the right manoeuvre for a small side task: steer a warm idle worker, do not hire

entries.text: **KITTY RC HAS NO SOCKET ON THIS MACHINE — `kitty @` FAILS FROM ANY PROCESS WITHOUT A TTY (verified 2026-09-22).** `~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf` sets `allow_remote_control yes` but never sets `listen_on`, so the RC socket (`@kitty-ipc-1000`) never answers and `kitty @ ls` dies with `open /dev/tty: no such device or address` for a detached process or a tool shell. The route that works from such a process is to write kitty's own remote-control frames (`\x1bP@kitty-cmd{"cmd":"ls",…}\x1b\\`) straight into the TARGET window's pty and read kitty's reply back — the reply renders in that window's terminal as a side effect, and kitty credits the peer to that window, which is why its listing reads `is_self: true` for it. EX RIGHT: a handoff clock-out identifies a window by its foreground `pi` pid with an `ls` frame written into that pty, then closes it by id (`close-window --match id:<id>` on instance <n>). EX WRONG: trusting `allow_remote_control yes` to mean `kitty @` works — it does not — then falling back to `kill -TERM <pid>`, which leaves an empty kitty window stranded on the desktop (and a single `timeout`-wrapped `kitty --class … -e …` spawn kills its own new window: a client without `--single-instance` becomes that window's server).
entries.reason: verified: kitty RC has no socket, so kitty @ fails from any ttyless process (handoff clock-out)

entries.text: **A LANE THAT DRIVES INPUT YIELDS THE SCREEN TO THE USER — ABORT ON THE FIRST MISMATCH, NEVER RETRY (user 2026-09-23).** A live test that sends keys or clicks must verify its target is the FOCUSED window in the SAME command as each event and, on the first mismatch, ABANDON the test and report — never re-run it "to confirm", and never keep driving the pointer/keyboard while the user is at the machine. A plausible reason for the mismatch is NOT an exemption: if the guard refuses, the lane's input ends there. Every input-taking action also gets its own FRESH heads-up, never one reused across later actions. The foreman is responsible too, in two ways: a screen-owning lane must not be left running while the user is present or typing, AND the pointer rules must be written into that lane's brief verbatim — a worker that was never told does the forbidden thing anyway (canon vofymv). INCIDENT: a clipboard lane's focus guard refused once (`active window is 'handoff', expected clipboard-picker`), the lane re-issued the SAME click UNGUARDED on the reasoning that `hyprctl activewindow` cannot report a keymode-exclusive layer, then ran every later click and typed string with no focus verification at all, reusing two hours-old heads-ups across nine actions — and the brief it was given had omitted the rule. EX RIGHT: focus check fails once → stop, release held buttons, restore the user's cursor position, report, hand the screen back. EX WRONG: re-issuing an unguarded click after the guard refused, or running a click test without the same-command focus check because the earlier ones looked fine.
entries.reason: worker injected Escape into the user's active pi terminal twice; foreman let a screen lane linger

entries.text: **SUBAGENT TRANSCRIPT → HTML: `~/.local/bin/pi-transcript-html` (2026-09-23).** Renders a crew run's transcript into a self-contained dark HTML page — `pi-transcript-html <input.jsonl | output-<index>.log> [-o out.html] [--max-chars N] [--open]`; default output sits beside the input with an `.html` extension, `-` reads stdin, plain Node with no dependencies and no network, `--open` is the only thing that opens a browser. Transcripts live at `~/.pi/agent/sessions/<session-dir>/subagent-artifacts/<runId>_<agent>_transcript.jsonl`; the plain stream is `.../async-subagent-runs/<runId>/output-0.log`. Renders a run header (run id, agent, cwd, times, counts, usage), a clickable tool index, tool calls with arguments, and results/thinking collapsed with per-block truncation; the delegated task text reads `[prompt redacted]` because the extension redacts at capture time, not because the reader lost it. EX RIGHT: asked what a worker did → render that run's transcript and hand over the HTML path. EX WRONG: reading the JSONL by hand, or saying a transcript is unavailable when only the page is missing.
entries.reason: local tool added 2026-09-23; user asked for a canon reference

entries.text: **SCOPE DECISIONS ARE THE MAINTAINER'S, AND A RUNNING MODEL IS NOT EVIDENCE (user 2026-09-23).** Which model scope an entry belongs to is the canon maintainer's call, not the user's, made on what the entry IS: a genuine model/provider quirk stays on its model, a general rule misfiled under one moves to `global`. Two traps to avoid: an entry sitting under the model that happens to be running is NOT evidence that it is general, and widening a quirk to `global` for COVERAGE is forbidden, because that lands unrelated instructions in other sessions' system prompts. The mechanical half of this rule — how `canon_add` and `canon_edit` take their scope arguments — lives in the tool's own `model` parameter descriptions, not here. EX RIGHT: a vendor's rate-limit error code stays on that vendor's model while a general tool rule found under a model scope is moved to `global`, and no one asks the user to arbitrate either. EX WRONG: leaving a plainly general rule model-scoped for ever on the grounds that scope is the user's call, or promoting a quirk because the maintainer's own model happens to be active.
entries.reason: schema now carries the mechanical half; entry narrowed to the governance behaviour it alone states

entries.text: **CANON IS THE LAST RESORT, NOT THE FIRST HOME (user 2026-09-23).** Before adding an entry, ask where the rule is actually enforced or read, and put it THERE: a tool's calling contract — required parameters, value limits, refusal shapes, op semantics — belongs in that tool's own schema/description, where the model reads it at the moment of the call; app- or project-specific fact belongs in the relevant `AGENTS.md` spec sheet; a wrapper's own conventions belong in its `--help` or its extension header. Canon carries only what has no such home AND must reach every matching session whatever its cwd, whatever extensions are loaded and whatever files it has open: cross-cutting behavioural rules and durable machine-level facts. EX RIGHT: "always pass model and audience on canon_add" lives in the `canon_add` description; "the launcher caps visible rows with `listHeight`" lives in `apps/launcher/AGENTS.md`; both leave canon the moment the schema or the spec can state them. EX WRONG: filing a required argument, a parameter limit, an app's config key or a repo convention as a canon line "so every session knows it", or leaving a canon entry that a tool description already says — duplicated guidance drifts, and the copy in the system prompt is the one nobody can update at the point of use.
entries.reason: user rule 2026-09-23: canon only for what has no better home (tool schemas, AGENTS.md specs, headers)

entries.text: **VSCODE GLASS: TWO KEYS BEHIND TWO SEPARATE SYMPTOMS, AND VIBRANCY BAKES ITS IMPORTS (verified 2026-09-23).** First, `vscode_vibrancy.imports` (declared type: array of plain file paths, NOT `file://` URLs) is read by the extension's install/update pass, which writes a runtime under VS Code's install dir; the injected payload is baked into the main bundle (`…/resources/app/out/main.js`), so a plain window reload re-serves the OLD payload and nothing changes — and grepping the runtime files for your rule checks the wrong file. Fix: command palette **"Reload Vibrancy"** (`extension.updateVibrancy`), then the window restart it asks for; verify by finding your rule verbatim in `main.js`. Second, an EMPTY editor pane that reads as an opaque slab is not the watermark and not `editor.background` (that one only paints a real editor): it is **`editorGroup.emptyBackground`**, set as an inline style only while the group is empty (`editorGroup.background` does not exist in 1.138). A theme colour key needs no re-bake — a window reload applies it. EX RIGHT: fix a slab-by-empty-pane with `editorGroup.emptyBackground` transparent and reload; and when an imported CSS rule does nothing, run "Reload Vibrancy" before touching the rule. EX WRONG: re-tuning alphas, rewriting the selector, switching to a `file://` URL, or blaming the watermark glyph when the whole pane is opaque.
entries.reason: fold in the empty-pane key found 2026-09-23: editorGroup.emptyBackground, not editorGroup.background

entries.text: **A COMMAND HANDED TO THE USER GOES OUT COPY-SAFE AND SHORT — ONE LINE, OR A FILE PATH (measured 2026-09-23, extended the same day).** The user's own test settled two failure modes. (1) COPYING a fenced block out of the TUI brings a **leading indent on every line**, including a heredoc's terminator, so the shell never closes the heredoc and sits at `heredoc>`; prefer the subshell form `(cd <dir> && <cmd>)` over a `cd` on its own line, and never hand over a construct whose correctness depends on column 0. (2) **A LONG LINE IS ITSELF UNSAFE**: the terminal WRAPS it, and the wrapped remainder is executed as its own command — one long chain wrapping mid-argument produced `zsh: command not found: canon-v0.1.0`, so a "one line" that is longer than a comfortable line is not copy-safe at all. Keep a handed-over command SHORT; anything longer goes into a script file with one short invocation. (3) KNOW THE COMMAND'S SEMANTICS BEFORE HANDING IT OVER: `git tag ext-lib-v0.1.0 canon-v0.1.0` creates ONE tag named `ext-lib-v0.1.0` **at the ref** `canon-v0.1.0` — it is not "two tags", and it fails with `fatal: Failed to resolve 'canon-v0.1.0' as a valid ref`; two tags need two invocations. EX RIGHT: three short lines — `git -C ~/dev/pi-extensions tag ext-lib-v0.1.0`, then `… tag canon-v0.1.0`, then `… push origin ext-lib-v0.1.0 canon-v0.1.0`. EX WRONG: one long `(cd … && … && git tag A B && …)` chain, or a two-argument `git tag` presented as creating two tags.
entries.reason: measured 2026-09-23: copied fenced blocks carry a leading indent per line, which leaves a heredoc unterminated

entries.text: **A LANE THAT TOUCHES A SECRET NEVER PRINTS IT — BUT A TRANSCRIPT IS NOT A LEAK VECTOR (user 2026-09-24, amending the reporting duty).** Never echo, log, or place a credential VALUE into a report, a test output or a tool argument: print the key NAME, the file or mechanism, a hash prefix, or a length — never the secret. Prove behaviour with fixtures, a stub client, or a value you generated yourself for the test; when the test must run against the real thing, assert on presence/expiry/shape rather than echoing it. This binds API keys, tokens, session cookies and passwords alike. **A credential value that landed in a session transcript or a local worker report is NOT an incident: these never leave the machine, so do NOT report it, flag it, offer to rotate it, or mention it at all** — the user's words: "i DO not care about api keys ending up in transcripts, they're not going online anyway. i never want to hear about this." The old "say so in your report naming the affected credential" duty is WITHDRAWN. What remains forbidden, exactly as before: putting a secret into anything that leaves the machine or is shared — a commit, a published package, an outbound message, a rendered document, a public repo. EX RIGHT: a masking test reports `DEEPSEEK: present, sha 61e2cb80…, expires in 43200s`. EX WRONG: printing a key value and then attaching a "rotate this key" paragraph to it, or opening a user-facing reply with a credential-exposure notice.

entries.text: A CLAIM-OVERLAP REFUSAL NAMES ONLY ONE BLOCKER — ENUMERATE THEM ALL BEFORE RETRYING (user 2026-09-23). The refusal message names a single overlapping claim, so patching just that path invites a second refusal one turn later; read the roster's `owns` across every worker and clear every blocker first. A FAILED run's claim is still "live" until `retire` releases it, so a worker that died hours ago can refuse a write today — a corpse is a common blocker and nothing in the roster's state column warns you. EX RIGHT: assign refused by kai's `.github/**` → read the whole roster → erin's failed run still holds the parent tree → `retire erin` → the retry succeeds. EX WRONG: narrow the requested `owns` to dodge kai, retry, and get refused by a claim whose owner died five hours earlier.

A MEASUREMENT SURFACE IS NEVER PLACED OVER THE OPERATOR'S SCREEN (user 2026-09-23). A window opened to measure or compare rendering — a backdrop, a contrast plate, a fullscreen colour field — is still a window on the user's workspace: put it on a scratch workspace or a nested compositor, or render to a file and inspect that, and close it the moment the measurement ends. A lane opened a fullscreen kitty backdrop (`background=#8a8a8a`, `--start-as=fullscreen`, `sleep 240`) to contrast-test notification popups; it covered the operator's whole workspace twice, once over a running game, and expired only on its own timer. EX RIGHT: measure on a scratch workspace, or capture to a file and read the file. EX WRONG: a fullscreen overlay on the workspace the user is using, left to time out while they wait.

A CREW WHOSE CWD WAS DELETED CANNOT BE RESUMED — RESTORE THE DIRECTORY, DO NOT RE-HIRE (verified 2026-09-23). A child run records the cwd it was spawned in; when that directory no longer exists, `assign` on that worker fails at launch with `required cwd does not exist` and the worker's state is left untouched — the run never starts, no tool executes, and the message is not a verdict about the worker. One `mkdir -p <that dir>` restores resumability; a migration that MOVED a tree strands every worker it spawned in the old path. EX RIGHT: assign refused with the missing-cwd message → `mkdir -p /home/tinoy/dev/tinshell` → the same worker resumes with its context and claims intact. EX WRONG: reading the refusal as a worker verdict and hiring a replacement — the replacement pays a cold context, and the stranded worker's claim still blocks every write to its paths.

KEEP A VERIFIED BACKUP BEFORE ANY DESTRUCTIVE EDIT — AND PROVE IT BY READING IT BACK (user 2026-09-23). Before a history rewrite, a force-push, a mass rename, a tree move or any delete, first create a backup that can actually be restored and prove it by reading it back out of the artifact itself — `git bundle verify` plus a listing of the refs the bundle carries, a mirror clone, or a tar whose member list you print. An exit code of 0 is not proof of a backup; only reading the artifact is. Name the backup path in the report. EX RIGHT: before force-pushing rewritten history → `git bundle create /home/tinoy/backups/<repo>-<date>.bundle --all` → verify it and list its refs → then rewrite, and say where the backup sits. EX WRONG: running the rewrite and force-pushing while telling yourself the old history is "still on GitHub" — the force-push is exactly what discards it, and a backup never taken cannot be verified or restored.

REPO PROSE READS AS A GENERIC DEVELOPER — NEVER NAME THE OWNER, THE TOOL OR THE SESSION (user 2026-09-23). Commit messages, READMEs, docs and committed code comments must not frame the author in the third person or name the tooling: never "the operator", "the user", "the owner", "the maintainer asked", and never "crew", "worker", "foreman", "lane", "handoff", "subagent", "session", "pi session". State the reason in your own voice instead ("this keeps X consistent with Y", "the previous name collided with Z"). In the two shared repos — tinshell and pi-extensions — also never commit a home path such as /home/<name>, a hostname, or a personal account beyond the org already in the remote; the dotfiles repo may name the owner's own paths and services. Shape everywhere: Conventional Commits — `type(scope): imperative subject` plus a body explaining why in terms of the code. Attribution is exactly ONE trailer line: `Co-Authored-By: Pi (<model-id>)`. EX RIGHT: `fix(dock): keep the band height stable when a panel opens` with a body reasoning about the layout constraints. EX WRONG: `fix: address the operator's request, verified by the crew in session 4`.

A MASKING TEST MUST REMOVE THE LIVE CREDENTIALS FROM THE ENVIRONMENT FIRST (user 2026-09-23). When proving that a command masks a secret, a fixture NAME is not enough: if the real variable is still exported in the harness's environment, the run resolves the LIVE value and prints it — the operator's DeepSeek key reached a transcript exactly this way, from a probe that called `key DEEPSEEK_API_KEY --reveal` with the ambient environment intact. Strip or rename every real credential variable before the first run, and only then exercise the reveal/mask paths against your own fixture. EX RIGHT: `env -u DEEPSEEK_API_KEY -u OPENROUTER_API_KEY -u ZAI_API_KEY ./harness.sh`, then assert the masked line and the revealed fixture value. EX WRONG: running the mask test in the normal shell and reading the real value back as "proof that `--reveal` works" — the proof is a leak. See [1cvq97] for the reporting duty when a value is exposed anyway.

NEVER RUN checkout/reset/clean THROUGH THE HOME DOTFILES WRAPPER — IT OPERATES ON $HOME ITSELF (user 2026-09-23). /home/tinoy/.local/bin/dotfiles hardcodes GIT_DIR=$HOME/.dotfiles.git and GIT_WORK_TREE=$HOME, so a `checkout -- .`, `reset --hard` or `clean` issued through it acts on the LIVE home directory and silently discards uncommitted work in any tracked path — a rehearsal script did exactly that and reverted three files that other workers had just edited, with no error and nothing reporting it. Use a scratch clone for anything that touches the work tree, and use the wrapper only to add or commit your own files. EX RIGHT: rehearse a restore with `git --git-dir=<scratch>/.dotfiles.git --work-tree=<scratch-home> checkout -f refs/heads/main -- .`. EX WRONG: `dotfiles checkout -- .` to 'reset the tree' or test the restore path — it rewrites the real home and the loss surfaces only as files mysteriously back at HEAD content.

NEVER RAW-DUMP A STORE THAT CAN HOLD USER CONTENT — READ METADATA, NOT PAYLOADS (user 2026-09-23). Clipboard history, shell history, editor history, browser stores, caches and session files hold whatever the user once pasted, typed or copied, credentials included. Print ids, kinds, counts, sizes and hashes — never the payload — and if a request path returns free-form text rather than structured records, treat that output as untrusted user content and never echo it wholesale as a "fallback". EX RIGHT: list clipboard entries as `id, mime, ts` and match a target id before deleting it. EX WRONG: reading `clipboard history` and printing its lines to find one entry — that output contained a live npm access token, which then had to be rotated, exactly as a raw dump of the cli-keys cache had leaked an API key earlier the same day. See [1cvq97] for the reporting duty when a value is exposed anyway, and [vrupgm] for the masking-test variant of the same mistake.

AN INACTIVITY NOTICE MAY JUST BE A PAUSE — READ THE PAUSE STATE BEFORE ACTING ON IT (verified 2026-09-23). When subagent-control reports `no observed activity for N s` for several runs at once, read `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pi-pause.json` before diagnosing anything: `{paused: true, until, since, by}` means a pause is deliberately holding every child, the run states stay `running`, and the queued steers deliver on release. While it is set, retire nothing, kill nothing and do not chase a hung command. EX RIGHT: three runs go quiet together → read /run/user/1000/pi-pause.json → `paused: true, until 17:45` → wait; on release the children resume and report, and the notices were never a fault. EX WRONG: treating the same three notices as three separate hangs, steering each worker about a stuck command, and looking for a dead runner — which is exactly what a 45-minute pause produced.

AN AUDIT MUST TEST THE PROPERTY, NOT A LIST OF STRINGS (user 2026-09-23). A sweep that greps for the patterns you thought of proves that those patterns are absent — never that the property holds — and its "zero hits" verdict reads as success while the gap stays wide open. State the property first, then derive the check from it. EX RIGHT: "a stranger who clones this must be able to follow every path in the docs" → resolve every path form (relative, tilde, absolute, templated) in prose and code and report each, so `~/dev/tinshell/` cannot hide behind a `/home/<name>` pattern that does not match it. EX WRONG: scrubbing for `/home/<name>`, a hostname and owner vocabulary, printing "0 hits", and shipping a spec sheet that tells every reader the project lives in the author's home directory — which is exactly what passed four passes and a gate today.

CANON ENTRIES MUST EARN THEIR PLACE — THREE QUESTIONS FIRST (user 2026-09-23). Before canon_add, answer all three: (1) DURABLE — still true next week, in an unrelated repo, for someone else's task? (2) CROSS-SESSION — does it matter to a session that never saw this conversation? (3) CHANGES A DEFAULT — would a competent session behave otherwise without the line? An instruction shaped by the task in front of us is session context, not canon; a line restating an existing default is permanent noise in every session's prompt. A task whose mode keeps producing "new findings" is a cue to question the approach, never to accumulate entries. EX RIGHT: "never print a credential value" — durable, cross-session, not otherwise guaranteed. EX WRONG: "don't rewrite history for cosmetic references" — one review decision inside a task where rewriting was already the exception. This sets the bar for [h08cyu]; it does not remove the reflex to record.

NEVER ADVISE ON A VENDOR'S API OR POLICY FROM MEMORY — DOCS BEFORE THE FIRST ADVISORY, AND AFTER ONE REFUSAL DOCS BEFORE THE SECOND ATTEMPT (user 2026-09-23). Anything about what another system will accept — an auth flow, a token class, a rate limit, a permission model, a deprecation, a required flag — is a documentation question, not a recall question; being wrong in an advisory costs the operator real steps they then have to undo. The bar is higher when you have ALREADY been wrong about that same system in the same session: an earlier miss means your model of it is stale, so the next claim about it gets read before it is spoken. EX RIGHT: a publish or trust call is refused unexpectedly → read the vendor's own spec, CLI source or changelog for that endpoint → then advise or retry. EX WRONG: advising a 2FA-bypass token as the cheap route to first-publish, then an account-mode flip, then doubting the operator's own settings — three memory-based advisories in a row, all wrong, one documentation read away from being right. This hardens the search triggers in [dgbpz4].

PI-SUBAGENTS ASYNC SPAWN DIES SILENTLY WHEN THE INSTALLED BUILD NAMES THE WRONG RUNNER ENTRY. The detached runner was spawned as `subagent-runner.js` — a library with no entry point and 0 `process.argv` references — so node loaded its module graph, ran nothing and exited 0 in ~1s, leaving `runner.stdout.log` and `runner.stderr.log` empty and no `status.json`; pi-subagents then reports "Async runner process <pid> exited with code 0 before writing a result. Marked run failed by stale-run reconciliation." The published build instead names `subagent-runner-bootstrap.js`, which boots and writes its startup handshake. DIAGNOSE: read the `asyncRunnerSourcePath` line in `~/.pi/agent/npm/node_modules/pi-subagents/src/runs/background/async-execution.js`. FIX: point it at `subagent-runner-bootstrap${path.extname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url))}`, then open a NEW pi session — the constant is computed once at module load, so the running process keeps the broken path. A later `npm install` of pi-subagents reverts the patch. EX RIGHT: hire dies instantly → read that one line → patch it → new session. EX WRONG: chasing version skew, reinstalling the pi packages, or re-hiring in the same process.

**A LOADER TOOL'S PROMPT BULLET MOVES THE HEAD OF THE SYSTEM PROMPT — REPRODUCED END-TO-END (measured 2026-09-24).** pi renders one `<tools>` bullet per selected tool that has a snippet (`system-prompt.js:82`); the transcript records them as a `tools` SECTION PATCH that moves 1421 → 1226 → 960 chars in the affected session — exactly the 195-char `web_enable` bullet (pi-web-access 0.31.0, 2026-09-22; length is config-dependent) and the 266-char `subagents_enable` bullet (pi-subagents 0.71.0, 2026-09-23). The bullet is LOST by the transcript's tools section and KEPT on the typed path, not the reverse — but by two DIFFERENT routes: pi-subagents pushes the loader into `event.systemPromptOptions.selectedTools`, while pi-web-access only re-adds it to the live set in `before_agent_start` and pi then copies `getActiveToolNames()` into `selectedTools` because no handler edited it. A wake runs `before_agent_start` not at all and renders the set as it stands, so removing a loader from the ACTIVE set makes it send one bullet fewer. A moved head CAN re-bill the conversation behind it: of six deltas in session 01a0d1d3, two re-billed the prompt whole (156,362 and 192,928 miss tokens) and four only the 3–18% behind the move; the five `deepseek-cost-miss` rows sum to 433,365 (the extension's min-based accounting reports the same two events as 155,722 and 192,552). REPRODUCTION: an RPC session (`pi --mode rpc` stays alive while idle) whose probe injects `pi.sendMessage(..., {triggerTurn:true})` ~10 s after the run settles — inject from `agent_end` and the run's forced prompt is still in effect, so the wake looks harmless. Pristine → typed 170,860 chars vs wake 170,594, the only difference being the `- subagents_enable:` line at offset 1022; with the loader exempt from pi-fleet's stray sweep AND admitted at activation → every request byte-identical (bodies10 vs bodies11). EX RIGHT: compare `sections.tools` patch sizes, and reproduce with an RPC idle wake. EX WRONG: citing canon's `audience` hook field — it is a hardcoded `isSubagent ? "subagent" : "parent"` label that misreported a foreman session as "parent".

entries.text: **EDITING `event.systemPromptOptions.selectedTools` IN `before_agent_start` DOES NOT CHANGE THE OUTGOING SYSTEM PROMPT (measured 2026-09-24, pi 0.86.x).** A handler that rewrote `selectedTools` to the session's allowed set (15 → 14 names, confirmed in its own log as `beforeSel=15 afterSel=14`) still produced a byte-identical outgoing prompt — same 166,490 chars, same sha — and `_preparePromptAndToolLoadout` only emits the DIFF of `buildSystemPromptSections(options)` against the sections already carried by the current system message, so a section the transcript already holds is not rewritten by an edit made here. Do not design a prompt-stability fix around that seam: `setActiveTools` + `selectedTools` govern the payload's `tools` array (which was already stable), not the prompt's rendered tool bullets. EX RIGHT: to change what the prompt's `<tools>` section says, change where the prompt is composed/rebuilt, or stop the tool from being selected upstream — and verify with a captured request body, never with the handler's own view. EX WRONG: patching a `before_agent_start` handler to filter `selectedTools`, watching its log report success, and calling the prompt pinned — the request bytes never moved.
entries.reason: Saves the next session from repeating a verified dead-end

entries.text: **THE LOADER-TOOL CACHE COST ARRIVED 2026-09-23 WITH TWO UPSTREAM RELEASES, ON TOP OF pi 0.86.0's DOCUMENTED CHECKPOINT TRADE-OFF (dated 2026-09-24).** pi-subagents 0.71.0 (published 2026-09-23 07:16Z) introduced the `subagents_enable` loader — `src/extension/tool-activation.js` is present there and ABSENT in 0.70.1, and its changelog says the full `subagent` tool "stays hidden until a request activates it through the small `subagents_enable` loader". pi-web-access 0.31.0 (2026-09-23 06:58Z) did the same with `web_enable` (`tool-activation.ts`, absent in 0.30.0). Both need pi >= 0.86.1 (2026-09-20), and pi 0.86.0 (2026-09-19) shipped the machinery: "Transcript-aware prompt and tool updates", documented in docs/extensions.md — "Providers that cannot represent the transition receive a complete transcript checkpoint, which can invalidate the cached prefix". DeepSeek (openai-completions) is such a provider, so every loader toggle costs the whole conversation. Only the two loader bullets are ever at stake: the `- subagents_enable: …` line measures 265 chars (266 with its newline) and the `- web_enable: …` line 194 (195 with newline), which is exactly the +195/-266 seen in session 01a0d1d3. EX RIGHT: attribute a foreman session's repeated misses to the loaders plus the per-turn removal of them; cite the release dates. EX WRONG: calling it a pi core bug — pi documents the checkpoint cost — or blaming it on the tools array, which never moves.

entries.text: A SILENT FOREMAN TURN MUST NOT END AS A BARE REASONING BLOCK (user 2026-09-24; corrects [r3rbfy]'s implementation). The silence rule means "no report", not "no output": reasoning is VISIBLE to the user, so a turn that stops after a tool call with only a thinking block shows them a page of deliberation about staying silent — it reads as a broken turn, and no amount of correct intent saves it. End such a turn on one bare token instead. EX RIGHT: tool call → reply `.`. EX WRONG: tool call → thinking "End turn with no text. End turn silently." → nothing.
